title: Coldchain microbenchmark notebook: reproducible throughput and warmup tests
content:
Purpose and context:
This notebook collects a compact, reproducible methodology for exercising the serving runtime with a focus on cold->hot transitions, repeatability across runs, and identifying production-relevant bottlenecks. It complements our larger loadbench playbooks by isolating microbenchmarks that reveal kernel and priming behaviors that affect sustained throughput.

Why ‘coldchain’?
We use the term coldchain to describe a controlled sequence of cold starts and short-run traffic bursts that emulate real-world patterns where some fraction of requests experience cold path work (kernel init, memory pinning, KV cache misses). The goal is to measure how the runtime toggles between cold and hot performance and to quantify the time and token cost to reach steady throughput.

High-level goals:
- Produce repeatable runs with statistical signals (median, p50/p90/p99) for tokens/sec and tail latencies.
- Surface sources of throughput drift (kernel selection, CUDA context churn, PCIe stalls, thermal scaling).
- Measure the effect of priming policies (KV cache warm vs lazy, prefix caching) on throughput recovery.
- Provide actionable knobs for engineering: batch sizing, priming length, inter-burst spacing, process pinning.

Experiment design summary:
1) Deterministic seed and client config: each run uses a fixed RNG seed and a fixed request set (tokenized sequences) derived from a canonical corpus.
2) Cold chain sequence: repeat N cold sessions where a worker process is cold-started, receive a short batch of requests (S requests), then teardown. After N repetitions, run a long steady-load window to measure hot throughput.
3) Observability capture window: collect low-level GPU traces during cold sessions and high-level telemetry during steady state.
4) Repeatability: run full experiment M times across different nodes and average, report per-run variance.

Typical parameters (example):
- N (cold repetitions): 8
- S (requests per cold session): 6
- request token length distribution: 8% short(16), 50% medium(64), 42% long(256)
- steady-state duration: 600s
- inter-burst idle gap: 15s
- client RNG seed: 20241105
- concurrency during steady-state: 24 clients

Load generator config (example YAML snippet):
client:
  generator: bench-client-v2
  seed: 20241105
  request_set: s3://bench-seqs/coldchain-corpus-v3.txt
  inter_request_jitter_ms: 5
sequence:
  cold_repetitions: 8
  cold_session_requests: 6
  idle_gap_seconds: 15
steady:
  duration_seconds: 600
  concurrency: 24
  target_qps: null  # let client maintain concurrency-driven QPS

Data to capture per run:
- High-resolution timestamps for each request/response (client-side).
- Per-token generation time where available (runtime instrumented).
- Prometheus metrics: tokens_processed_total, request_count_total, request_duration_seconds_bucket, model_load_count, kv_cache_hit_ratio (if exported).
- GPU-level: nsys timeline, sm_efficiency, active_warps, achieved_occupancy, memory throughput, PCIe rx/tx rates (via nvidia-smi dmon or Nsight metrics).
- Host OS counters: CPU steal, softirq, context-switches, disk IO (to catch swap).
- Environmental telemetry: GPU temperature, power draw.

Profiling recipe (lightweight + deep):
A) Lightweight run (default):
- Capture Prometheus metrics and client logs.
- Run for the full coldchain sequence + steady window.
- Produce p50/p90/p99 for latency and tokens/sec time series.
- Use this to detect runs with anomalous drift; discard if deviant >10% from median.

B) Deep dive (for flagged runs):
- Re-run the same profile but attach Nvidia Nsight Systems (nsys) with sampling on a single node: nsys profile --output=coldchain-REPL-%h --sample=cpu --trace=cuda,cudnn,osrt --duration=full
- Collect CUPTI-derived SM metrics and per-kernel timelines.
- Correlate kernel shapes to request types (short/medium/long).

Noise and variance mitigation checklist:
- Disable frequency governors for benchmark hosts (set CPUs to performance).
- Fix GPU persistence daemon states where applicable; run after a 15-minute idle to clear thermal history if comparing across days.
- Use an isolated NIC and avoid cross-traffic in lab clusters; record background pps/bytes to reject noisy runs.
- Synchronize clocks across client and server with ntp/chrony; verify offset < 5ms.
- Run battery of at least 5 full coldchain experiments per node to estimate within-node variance.

Priming strategies to evaluate:
- No priming (baseline): measure pure cold chain cost.
- Full prefix priming: send a long prefix to populate KV cache prior to burst. Measure tokens/sec improvement and extra token cost.
- Partial priming: warm only top-K layers' KV or run a synthetic short request designed to occupy most-common keyspace.
- Warm pool vs ephemeral workers: measure difference when workers are re-used across sessions vs process-per-session.

Key hypotheses to validate with coldchain microbenchmarks:
1) Kernel init costs (first-run cudnn/cuda kernels) are a major contributor to early cold sessions for long sequences. Test by comparing runs with env var to force preloading vs lazy load.
2) KV cache sparsity on realistic prefixes causes a measurable throughput ramp; quantify tokens and requests required to reach 90% of hot throughput.
3) Host-level interrupts or PCIe stalls coincide with throughput dips; detect via cross-correlation of PCIe tx/rx and tokens/sec.
4) Thermal or power throttling rarely shows within short bursts but can appear if we sweep a large number of cold sessions back-to-back; track temp/power curve.

Analysis primitives (what we compute from raw traces):
- Warmup curve: tokens/sec vs elapsed time since first cold session (smooth with rolling 5s window).
- Priming cost: extra tokens generated exclusively for warmup divided by delta in steady tokens/sec.
- Recovery half-life: time to climb from 10% to 50% and 50% to 90% of steady throughput.
- Kernel waterfall: stacked timeline of major GPU kernels annotated with request type.
- Run-to-run variance: coefficient of variation for median tokens/sec across M runs.

Troubleshooting heuristics (common failure modes):
- Symptom: large variance between apparently identical runs. Check: thermal history, background host load, scheduler preemption.
- Symptom: slow cold ramp but fast subsequent recovery. Check: model file mmap behavior, filesystem cache misses, page fault counts.
- Symptom: occasional multi-second stalls. Check: PCIe errors, driver messages (dmesg), OOM killers, cgroup memory reclaim.

Conventions and recording format:
- Each experiment directory must include: params.yaml (the client config), seqs_hash.txt (sha256 of the request set), run.log (client stdout/stderr), prometheus-snapshot.json, nsys.tar (if captured), client-trace.jsonl (per-request lines).
- Use a consistent run id prefix: coldchain-<node>-<date>-<runnum>. Example: coldchain-a100-20250120-r03

Short reproducibility checklist for run authors:
- [ ] Commit seed and sequences to s3 and record seqs_hash.txt
- [ ] Boot the node into performance mode and record kernel version / driver version
- [ ] Ensure no other experiments on the same NIC / GPU; snapshot nvidia-smi topo
- [ ] Run lightweight capture; inspect p50/p90 for outliers; if OK, proceed to deep Nsight capture

Quick example interpretation (hypothetical):
- Run summary: median tokens/sec steady = 12.3k t/s, coldchain initial burst median = 2.1k t/s, recovery half-life = 27s, extra priming tokens = 9% of steady workload.
- Investigation: nsys showed two heavy kernels during cold sessions with long host-side memcpy and cudnn init calls; file-backed model mmap caused page faults in first two cold sessions. Fix: pre-mmap model files during node start.

Open questions and next experiments:
- How does quantized kernel selection interact with coldchain? (measure cold ramp for 8-bit vs 16-bit variants).
- How much benefit is gained by lightweight persistent warmers that continuously send small priming requests vs on-demand priming? Cost/benefit analysis required.
- Can we design a synthetic request distribution that approximates real customer prefix diversity to stress KV cache churn more realistically?

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
- Nsight quick capture: nsys profile --trace=cuda,cudnn,osrt --output=/tmp/nsys-coldchain --wait=100 -t 0 --capture-range=process:PID
- GPU metrics sampling: nvidia-smi dmon -s pucmt -d 1 > gpu-dmon.log  (then parse sm, mem, temp)
- Host counters (Linux perf): perf stat -e context-switches,cpu-clock,cycles,instructions,cache-misses -p <server-pid> -- sleep 600
- Prometheus scrape snapshot: curl -sS http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query?query=up > prometheus-up.json

Notes to reviewer:
This notebook is intentionally compact; it should serve as a reproducible checklist and a small experiment harness spec for on-call and SRE investigations. If accepted, we should add a small runner script to repo redwood/bench-harness that generates the params.yaml and archives artifacts in the required directory layout.
